title: Tuck In the Moon

topics.value_lesson: Winding down: all the wild moon games end in snuggling, soft voices, and feeling safe under the gentle glow

spine: A small child in footie pajamas plays bigger and bigger good-night games with the moon until the only thing left to do is tuck the moon in the way the child knows best.

segments.text: Moonlight spills across {hero_name}'s blanket in a long white stripe. Outside the window, the moon hangs over the rooftops, glowing like a big banana. "Good night, Moon!" says {hero_name}, and waves. The moon glows brighter! So {hero_name} waves both arms. Brighter! Both arms and one leg! Grandma windmills too, like a silly machine. Biscuit the cat meows at the window. "Grandma, look," says {hero_name}. "The moon is a banana. It must be hungry!"

"First, a cracker!" says {hero_name}, holding it up to the window. The moon just glows. "Then the banana, because it matches!" But when {hero_name} turns around, the plate is empty. Biscuit the cat licks his whiskers. Crumbs! "You ate the moon's snack!" giggles {hero_name}. Biscuit purrs. The moon hangs there, still hungry, still glowing. "The whole jar!" says {hero_name}. Grandma helps lift it, heavy and wobbly, up to the windowsill. "Eat up, Moon!"

"I'll catch it!" whispers {hero_name}. The moonbeam slides across the floor like a silver snail. Step on it! It slips away. Grab it with both hands! It wiggles free. Scoop it in the jar! The jar stays empty. But look - the moonbeam lands smack on Biscuit the cat. Biscuit glows! He purrs louder and louder, a soft rumbling cat-lamp in the dark. "The moon knows the softest spot," laughs Grandma. {hero_name} pats the warm, glowing cat. The moonbeam stays right there, on Biscuit's stripey back.

Grandma pours more warm milk. "Here's the thing, little one," she says. "The moon's glow is borrowed. Every evening, the sun tucks its light into the moon's pocket, like handing over a night-light. The moon carries it all night, watching every house." {hero_name} gasps. "The sun and moon take turns?" Biscuit purrs. Then {hero_name} sits up tall. "Grandma! If the moon watches us all night... somebody has to tuck IT in!" Grandma raises her mug. "How do you tuck in something so big and glowy?"

"My blanket!" says {hero_name}. Grandma helps drape it over the windowsill, like the moon's very own covers. Then {hero_name} sings. Loud! "GOOD NIGHT, MOON!" Too loud for bedtime. Softer now. Softer. A whisper. "Good night, moon." The glow settles over the room like a blanket of its own. {hero_name} climbs into bed under one white stripe. "Good night, Sun, wherever you're sleeping." And one small moonbeam stays on the blanket. All night long.

"My pillow!" says {hero_name}, marching it to the window. On the sill it goes, so the moon has somewhere to rest its face. Biscuit claims half of it. Official pillow-guard. Pat, pat. "Good night, Moon. Good night, Sun, wherever you're sleeping." Grandma carries {hero_name} to bed, and look - the moonbeam has saved a stripe of glow across the blanket, tucked in neat. The moon watches every house on the street. So nobody sleeps alone. Not ever.

choice_points.question: "Well, little moon-keeper," says Grandma, sipping her warm milk, "if that banana moon is hungry, shall we feed it a bedtime snack - or shall we try to catch that slippery moonbeam sliding across the floor?"

gathered_but_unused: The moon looks like it follows you when you walk or ride in the car at night.
The moon does not make its own light; it shines because the sun lights it up like a mirror.
The moon can look like different shapes on different nights — a big round circle or a curved banana slice.
The moon has bumpy spots and round dents called craters on its face.
You can sometimes see the moon in the daytime, faint and pale in the blue sky.
The moon is very far away — so far that a rocket ship has to fly for days to get there.
The moon goes around and around the Earth, like a slow, quiet merry-go-round.
The moon's soft glow is gentle enough to look at — it never hurts your eyes.
